course.title: Intermediate Web Development
course.description: A comprehensive 30-part intermediate course for developers ready to move beyond basics. Covers advanced HTML5 APIs, CSS architecture & modern layout systems, deep JavaScript internals, asynchronous patterns, browser APIs, performance optimization, web security, TypeScript, tooling, and Progressive Web Apps. Assumes solid HTML/CSS/JS fundamentals.

parts.partTitle: Part 1: Semantic HTML Deep Dive & Document Outline

blocks.value: Sectioning Elements, Heading Outlines & SEO Structure

Beyond basic `<header>` and `<footer>`, HTML5 sectioning elements (`<section>`, `<article>`, `<aside>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`) create an implicit document outline that search engines and assistive technologies use to understand page hierarchy. The **HTML5 Document Outline Algorithm** means each sectioning root can have its own `<h1>`, but for backward compatibility and SEO, maintain a single logical heading hierarchy per page. Use `aria-labelledby` to explicitly associate sections with their headings.

blocks.output: Creates a proper document outline with landmarks (banner, navigation, main, article, complementary, contentinfo) for screen readers and search crawlers.

blocks.question: Which attribute explicitly connects a section to its heading for assistive technologies?
blocks.explanation: `aria-labelledby` references the ID of an element (usually a heading) that serves as the accessible name for the section, landmark, or region.

parts.partTitle: Part 2: HTML5 Canvas & SVG Graphics

blocks.value: Programmatic Drawing vs. Declarative Vector Graphics

The **Canvas API** provides a bitmap drawing surface via JavaScript — ideal for games, image editing, and real-time data visualization where you need pixel control. **SVG** is a declarative XML-based vector format that scales infinitely and remains accessible and styleable with CSS. Choose Canvas for high-performance pixel manipulation; choose SVG for icons, charts, and illustrations that need to scale or remain interactive via DOM events.

<!-- SVG: Declarative, DOM-accessible, scalable -->
<svg width="200" height="200" viewBox="0 0 100 100" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="grad" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="100%">
      <stop offset="0%" style="stop-color:#6366f1;stop-opacity:1" />
      <stop offset="100%" style="stop-color:#a855f7;stop-opacity:1" />
    </linearGradient>
  </defs>
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="url(#grad)" />
  <text x="50" y="55" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-size="12">SVG</text>
</svg>

<!-- Canvas: Pixel-based, JavaScript-driven -->
<canvas id="drawCanvas" width="400" height="200"></canvas>

blocks.output: SVG renders a gradient circle with text. Canvas renders a gradient box with text and an animated green circle moving horizontally.

blocks.question: Which graphics technology is resolution-independent, DOM-accessible, and styleable with CSS?
blocks.explanation: SVG is vector-based XML markup. Every element exists in the DOM, can have event listeners, and scales to any resolution without pixelation.

parts.partTitle: Part 3: Advanced Forms & Constraint Validation API

blocks.value: Programmatic Validation, FormData, and File Handling

Modern forms go far beyond the `required` attribute. The **Constraint Validation API** gives JavaScript access to each form element's validity state via `element.validity`, `element.checkValidity()`, and `element.setCustomValidity()`. The `FormData` interface programmatically constructs key-value pairs for submission, including files. Use the `accept` attribute and `FileReader` API to preview images before upload.

blocks.output: Custom validation messages on blur. Image preview appears before upload. FormData logs all fields including file metadata on submit.

blocks.question: Which method on a form element triggers the browser to show its built-in validation UI?
blocks.explanation: `reportValidity()` both checks validity AND shows the browser's native validation tooltip. `checkValidity()` only returns a boolean without showing UI.

parts.partTitle: Part 4: Media APIs & Responsive Images

blocks.value: srcset, sizes, Picture Element & Video API

Serving the same 2000px image to mobile and desktop wastes bandwidth. The `srcset` attribute lets browsers choose the optimal image resolution based on device pixel density (`1x`, `2x`, `3x`) or viewport width. The `<picture>` element enables **art direction** — completely different images for different breakpoints. For video, the HTML5 Media API exposes `play()`, `pause()`, and events like `timeupdate` for custom players.

blocks.output: Browser selects optimal image resolution. Picture element shows mobile or desktop banner. Custom video player with play/pause and seek bar.

blocks.question: Which HTML element is used for art direction — showing completely different images at different breakpoints?
blocks.explanation: The `<picture>` element contains multiple `<source>` elements with media queries, allowing different images (cropped, different aspect ratios) for different devices.

parts.partTitle: Part 5: Web Storage, IndexedDB & Cache API

blocks.value: Structured Offline Storage Beyond localStorage

`localStorage` and `sessionStorage` are synchronous and limited to ~5MB of strings. **IndexedDB** is an asynchronous, transactional, NoSQL database capable of storing megabytes of structured data, files, and blobs. It uses object stores, indexes, and versioned schemas. The **Cache API** (used by Service Workers) stores HTTP request/response pairs for offline access.

blocks.output: IndexedDB stores task objects with an index on priority. Cache API pre-caches static assets for offline use.

blocks.question: Which storage API is transactional, asynchronous, and capable of storing structured objects and files?
blocks.explanation: IndexedDB is a low-level API for client-side storage of significant amounts of structured data, including files and blobs. It uses indexes for high-performance searches.

parts.partTitle: Part 6: CSS Architecture — BEM, SMACSS & Design Tokens

blocks.value: Scalable CSS Methodologies and Token Systems

As projects grow, CSS becomes unmaintainable without architecture. **BEM (Block Element Modifier)** names classes as `.block__element--modifier` to create strict component boundaries. **SMACSS** categorizes rules into Base, Layout, Module, State, and Theme. **Design Tokens** are platform-agnostic variables (colors, spacing, typography) stored as JSON and compiled to CSS variables, ensuring consistency across design systems.

blocks.output: BEM creates predictable, scoped class names. No specificity wars, no unexpected cascade side effects.
Design tokens create a single source of truth. Changing --color-primary updates the entire application.

blocks.question: In BEM methodology, what separator is used between a Block and its Modifier?
blocks.explanation: BEM uses double underscores `__` for Elements (`.block__element`) and double hyphens `--` for Modifiers (`.block--modifier` or `.block__element--modifier`).

parts.partTitle: Part 7: Advanced CSS Selectors & Pseudo-Classes

blocks.value: :is(), :where(), :has(), and Complex Combinators

Modern CSS selectors dramatically reduce specificity bloat and repetition. `:is()` matches any selector in its list (useful for grouping), but it **adopts the specificity of the most specific argument**. `:where()` is identical to `:is()` but always has **zero specificity**, making it perfect for reset stylesheets. `:has()` is the long-awaited **parent selector** — it styles an element based on its children. Combine these with combinators (`>`, `+`, `~`) for surgical targeting without extra classes.

blocks.output: Headings with links are purple. Parent cards adapt styling based on child content. Input hints animate when focused. Error messages appear only when input is invalid.

blocks.question: Which pseudo-class functions like `:is()` but always has zero specificity?
blocks.explanation: `:where()` takes a selector list and matches any element matched by the selectors, but its specificity is always zero, unlike `:is()` which takes the specificity of its most specific argument.

parts.partTitle: Part 8: CSS Custom Properties, Theming & Dark Mode

blocks.value: Dynamic Variables, Color Schemes, and Runtime Theming

CSS Custom Properties (variables) cascade and inherit like any other property, making them more powerful than preprocessor variables. Define a theme on `:root`, override it with `data-theme` attributes, and respect the user's OS preference with `prefers-color-scheme`. Use `color-scheme: light dark` to enable native form control theming. JavaScript can toggle themes by setting attributes or classes.

blocks.output: Light theme by default. Dark theme via data attribute or OS preference. Smooth transitions between modes.
Theme toggle button switches between light and dark, persists choice in localStorage, and respects OS preference on first visit.

blocks.question: Which CSS media query detects if the user has requested a dark color scheme in their operating system?
blocks.explanation: `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` matches when the user's OS is set to dark mode, allowing websites to adapt automatically.

parts.partTitle: Part 9: CSS Grid Areas, Subgrid & Container Queries

blocks.value: Named Grid Regions, Nested Grids, and Component-Based Responsiveness

CSS Grid **named areas** (`grid-template-areas`) make complex layouts readable and maintainable. **Subgrid** (Firefox + Safari + Chrome 117+) allows nested grids to inherit track definitions from their parent, aligning grandchild elements across unrelated components. **Container Queries** (`@container`) finally enable components to respond to their own width rather than the viewport, solving the 'card in sidebar vs card in main' problem.

blocks.output: Dashboard has named regions. Form rows align labels and inputs using parent's grid tracks. Product cards stack vertically when their container is narrow, regardless of screen size.

blocks.question: Which CSS feature allows a nested grid to use the track sizing of its parent grid?
blocks.explanation: `grid-template-columns: subgrid` makes the child grid use the parent's column tracks, enabling perfect alignment of deeply nested elements.

parts.partTitle: Part 10: CSS Functions, Logical Properties & @layer

blocks.value: clamp(), min(), max(), aspect-ratio, @property, and Cascade Layers

Modern CSS functions enable fluid design without media queries. `clamp(min, preferred, max)` sets a value with a floor and ceiling. `min()` and `max()` compare values. `aspect-ratio` maintains proportions for images and containers. `@property` registers custom properties for type-safe animation. **Cascade Layers** (`@layer`) explicitly control the specificity hierarchy of entire stylesheets, making framework overrides predictable.

blocks.output: Typography scales fluidly. Container respects max-width. Article adapts padding for RTL languages. Video wrapper maintains 16:9. Custom property animates smoothly. Cascade layers prevent specificity wars.

blocks.question: Which CSS function sets a preferred value with a minimum floor and maximum ceiling?
blocks.explanation: `clamp(MIN, VAL, MAX)` resolves to VAL unless it falls below MIN or exceeds MAX, making it perfect for fluid typography and spacing.

parts.partTitle: Part 11: CSS Houdini, Scroll Animations & View Transitions

blocks.value: Programmable CSS, Native Scroll-Driven Animations, and Page Transitions

**CSS Houdini** exposes parts of the CSS engine to JavaScript via the Typed OM, Paint API, and Layout API. The **Scroll-driven Animations** API (Chrome 115+) animates elements based on scroll position using `animation-timeline: scroll()` instead of JavaScript scroll listeners. The **View Transitions API** (Chrome 111+) enables smooth morphing animations between DOM states during SPA navigation.

blocks.output: Image moves slowly as user scrolls. Page transitions fade smoothly between states.
If supported, the browser captures the old state, morphs elements to the new state, and plays the CSS-defined transition.

blocks.question: Which CSS property connects an animation to the scroll position of a container instead of time?
blocks.explanation: `animation-timeline: scroll()` links an animation's progress directly to the scroll progress of a container, eliminating the need for JavaScript scroll event listeners.

parts.partTitle: Part 12: ES6+ Modules, Scope & Strict Mode

blocks.value: Module Systems, Block Scoping, and Temporal Dead Zone

ES6 Modules (`import`/`export`) provide true encapsulation with private module scope, unlike global script tags. `let` and `const` create **block-scoped** variables that exist only within their nearest `{}` pair. `const` prevents reassignment of the binding, though object properties remain mutable. Variables declared with `let`/`const` suffer from the **Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)** — they cannot be accessed before their declaration line, unlike hoisted `var`.

blocks.output: Modules encapsulate code. Named exports are tree-shakeable. Default exports are imported without curly braces.
var is hoisted to undefined. let/const throw ReferenceError in TDZ. Block scopes create independent bindings. const objects remain mutable internally.

blocks.question: What happens when you access a `let` variable before its declaration line?
blocks.explanation: let and const variables exist in the Temporal Dead Zone from the start of their block until their declaration is executed. Accessing them during TDZ throws a ReferenceError.

parts.partTitle: Part 13: Destructuring, Spread, Rest & Template Literals

blocks.value: Concise Data Extraction and Collection Manipulation

Destructuring unpacks values from arrays and objects into distinct variables. The **rest syntax** (`...`) collects remaining properties into a new object/array. The **spread syntax** (`...`) expands iterables into individual elements. Combined with default values and renaming, these features eliminate verbose property access. Template literals (backticks) support multi-line strings and embedded expressions via `${}`.

blocks.output: Destructuring extracts nested values cleanly. Rest collects leftovers. Spread clones and merges. Tagged templates enable custom string processing.

blocks.question: Which syntax collects the remaining un-destructured array elements into a new array?
blocks.explanation: The rest pattern `const [a, b, ...rest] = arr` packs all remaining elements after a and b into the `rest` array. Do not confuse it with spread, which unpacks.

parts.partTitle: Part 14: Map, Set, WeakMap & WeakSet

blocks.value: Specialized Collections for Performance and Privacy

`Map` stores key-value pairs where keys can be any type (including objects), maintains insertion order, and provides O(1) lookups. `Set` stores unique values. `WeakMap` and `WeakSet` are variants where keys must be objects and are held by **weak references** — they do not prevent garbage collection. This makes WeakMap perfect for private data associated with DOM nodes or class instances without memory leaks.

blocks.output: Map handles object keys. Set deduplicates. WeakMap hides password from external access and allows garbage collection if the instance is no longer referenced.

blocks.question: Which collection uses weak references for keys, allowing garbage collection when no other references exist?
blocks.explanation: WeakMap keys are held weakly. If the key object is no longer referenced elsewhere, the entry is eligible for garbage collection, preventing memory leaks in long-running apps.

parts.partTitle: Part 15: Closures, Currying & Functional Patterns

blocks.value: Lexical Scoping, Partial Application, and Higher-Order Functions

A **closure** is a function that retains access to its outer lexical scope even after the outer function has returned. This enables data privacy, factory functions, and stateful modules. **Currying** transforms a function with multiple arguments into a sequence of functions each taking a single argument. **Higher-order functions** accept or return other functions, enabling composition patterns like `pipe` and `compose`.

blocks.output: Counter encapsulates state. Currying creates specialized functions. Pipe chains transformations. Memoized fibonacci runs in milliseconds.

blocks.question: What JavaScript feature allows an inner function to access variables from its outer function after the outer function has completed execution?
blocks.explanation: A closure captures the lexical environment of its birth place, maintaining references to outer variables as long as the inner function exists.

parts.partTitle: Part 16: Prototypes, Classes & Object Patterns

blocks.value: Inheritance, Encapsulation, and Factory vs Constructor Patterns

JavaScript uses **prototypal inheritance** — objects delegate to other objects via the internal `[[Prototype]]` chain. The `class` syntax is syntactic sugar over constructor functions and prototypes. Understanding `Object.create()`, `Object.setPrototypeOf()`, and the difference between own properties and inherited properties is crucial for debugging and library development. **Factory functions** with closures often provide better encapsulation than classes.

blocks.output: Rex barks. Tesla drives with battery percentage. Factory user tracks private login count.

blocks.question: Which method creates a new object with a specified prototype object?
blocks.explanation: `Object.create(proto)` creates a new object whose internal [[Prototype]] is set to the provided proto object, establishing the inheritance chain.

parts.partTitle: Part 17: Generators, Iterators & Async Iterators

blocks.value: Lazy Evaluation, Custom Iteration, and Streaming Data

**Generators** (`function*`) are functions that can pause and resume execution, yielding multiple values lazily via the `yield` keyword. They implement the **Iterator protocol** (`next()`, `done`, `value`) automatically. **Async generators** (`async function*`) yield Promises, enabling consumption of streaming data with `for await...of`. This is ideal for paginated APIs, real-time logs, and large datasets that shouldn't be loaded entirely into memory.

blocks.output: Generator produces IDs on demand. Range is spreadable into an array. Async generator streams paginated users without loading all pages at once.

blocks.question: Which keyword inside a generator function pauses execution and returns a value to the caller?
blocks.explanation: `yield` pauses the generator and returns the value. The next call to `.next()` resumes execution from where it left off.

parts.partTitle: Part 18: Modern Syntax — Optional Chaining, Nullish Coalescing & Logical Assignment

blocks.value: Defensive Property Access and Default Values

**Optional chaining** (`?.`) safely accesses nested properties, returning `undefined` if any part of the chain is nullish instead of throwing. **Nullish coalescing** (`??`) returns the right-hand operand only if the left is `null` or `undefined` (not `0`, `''`, or `false`). Logical assignment operators (`||=`, `&&=`, `??=`) combine logical operations with assignment for concise defaults and conditional updates.

blocks.output: Safe nested access without try/catch. Nullish coalescing preserves 0 and empty strings. Logical assignment provides concise conditional updates.

blocks.question: Which operator returns the right-hand value only if the left-hand value is `null` or `undefined`?
blocks.explanation: The nullish coalescing operator `??` only falls back for `null` or `undefined`, unlike `||` which falls back for all falsy values (0, '', false, NaN).

parts.partTitle: Part 19: The JavaScript Event Loop Deep Dive

blocks.value: Call Stack, Task Queue, Microtasks, and the Rendering Pipeline

JavaScript is single-threaded but asynchronous through the **Event Loop**. Synchronous code runs on the **Call Stack**. Asynchronous callbacks are queued: **Macrotasks** (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O) go to the Task Queue, while **Microtasks** (`Promise.then`, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`) go to the Microtask Queue. After each macrotask, the engine drains the entire microtask queue before rendering or picking the next macrotask. Understanding this order prevents race conditions and layout thrashing.

blocks.output: Demonstrates that all microtasks (including nested ones) execute before the next macrotask.
Bad example forces 100 synchronous reflows. Good example batches reads and schedules writes before the next paint.

blocks.question: Which queue is completely drained before the browser proceeds to the next macrotask or render?
blocks.explanation: The event loop processes one macrotask, then drains the entire microtask queue, then checks for rendering opportunities. This gives microtasks higher priority.

parts.partTitle: Part 20: Promises Advanced & Async Patterns

blocks.value: Promise Combinators, Error Handling, and Sequential vs Parallel Execution

Beyond `Promise.all()`, modern JavaScript provides `Promise.allSettled()` (waits for all, never rejects), `Promise.race()` (settles with the first to complete), and `Promise.any()` (fulfills with the first success, or rejects with an AggregateError). Use `AbortController` to cancel in-flight `fetch` requests. For sequential async operations, use `for...of` with `await` rather than `forEach` (which ignores async returns).

blocks.output: allSettled reports all outcomes. any returns first success. AbortController cancels slow requests. Sequential loop preserves order.

blocks.question: Which Promise combinator waits for all promises to settle and returns an array of {status, value|reason} objects?
blocks.explanation: Promise.allSettled() never rejects. It returns an array where each item indicates whether the corresponding promise was fulfilled or rejected, along with its value or reason.

parts.partTitle: Part 21: Fetch API, Streams & CORS

blocks.value: Modern HTTP Requests, Response Streams, and Cross-Origin Security

The `fetch()` API is promise-based and more flexible than `XMLHttpRequest`. It supports streaming via `response.body` (a ReadableStream), allowing you to process large responses chunk by chunk without buffering everything in memory. **CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)** is a browser security mechanism. Preflight `OPTIONS` requests are sent for non-simple requests (custom headers, methods other than GET/POST, certain content types). The server must respond with appropriate `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers.

blocks.output: Fetch sends JSON with auth headers. Streaming reader processes response body incrementally without loading entire file into RAM.

blocks.value:
# CORS Preflight Request
OPTIONS /api/data HTTP/1.1
Origin: https://frontend.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
Access-Control-Request-Headers: X-Request-ID

# CORS Preflight Response
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://frontend.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, X-Request-ID
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
blocks.output: Browser automatically sends OPTIONS preflight. Server must whitelist origin, methods, and headers for the actual request to proceed.

blocks.question: Which HTTP method does the browser automatically use for CORS preflight requests?
blocks.explanation: For non-simple cross-origin requests, the browser sends an OPTIONS preflight request to ask the server for permission before sending the actual request.

parts.partTitle: Part 22: DOM Events — Capture, Bubble, Delegate

blocks.value: Event Phases, Propagation Control, and Memory-Efficient Listeners

DOM events travel through three phases: **Capture** (down from window to target), **Target** (the element itself), and **Bubble** (up from target to window). Most handlers listen during the bubble phase. Use `event.stopPropagation()` to prevent further propagation, and `event.preventDefault()` to cancel default browser behavior. **Event Delegation** attaches a single listener to a parent to handle events from multiple children — essential for dynamic lists and memory management.

blocks.output: Events flow capture -> target -> bubble. Delegation handles clicks on dynamically added items. Custom events enable decoupled architecture.

blocks.question: What is the primary benefit of event delegation over attaching individual listeners to each child element?
options: It reduces memory usage and automatically handles dynamically added elements
blocks.correctAnswer: It reduces memory usage and automatically handles dynamically added elements
blocks.explanation: A single parent listener uses less memory than N child listeners. Because the event bubbles up, elements added after the listener is attached are still handled automatically.

parts.partTitle: Part 23: Browser Observers API

blocks.value: IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver, and MutationObserver

Polling the DOM in scroll or resize events causes performance issues. Modern browsers provide **Observer APIs** for efficient, event-driven DOM monitoring. **IntersectionObserver** detects when elements enter/leave the viewport — perfect for lazy loading, infinite scroll, and analytics. **ResizeObserver** watches element content box changes (not just window). **MutationObserver** reacts to DOM tree changes (added/removed nodes, attribute changes) without polling.

blocks.output: Images load only when near viewport. Widgets adapt class when resized. Console logs when new items are injected into the DOM.

blocks.question: Which Observer is designed to detect when an element enters or leaves the browser viewport?
blocks.explanation: IntersectionObserver efficiently tracks whether a target element intersects with a root container (typically the viewport), enabling lazy loading and visibility-based analytics.

parts.partTitle: Part 24: Web Components — Custom Elements & Shadow DOM

blocks.value: Encapsulated, Reusable HTML Components Without Frameworks

Web Components are a suite of native browser APIs for creating reusable custom elements. **Custom Elements** let you define new HTML tags with JavaScript classes extending `HTMLElement`. The **Shadow DOM** creates an encapsulated DOM subtree with scoped CSS that cannot leak out or be pierced by global styles. Combined with **HTML Templates** (`<template>` and `<slot>`), you get framework-independent components that work in any app.

blocks.output: Defines <user-card> element with scoped styles, slots for content projection, and lifecycle hooks.

blocks.value: Last active: 2 hours ago
blocks.output: Renders a styled card with an avatar image slotted into the named slot, and default paragraph content in the unnamed slot.

blocks.question: Which method creates an encapsulated DOM subtree inside a custom element?
blocks.explanation: `element.attachShadow({mode: 'open'})` creates a ShadowRoot. Styles inside the shadow tree are scoped and do not leak to the outside document.

parts.partTitle: Part 25: Service Workers, Cache Strategies & PWA Basics

blocks.value: Offline-First Architecture and Background Sync

A **Service Worker** is a script that runs in a separate thread, intercepting network requests and enabling offline experiences. It has a lifecycle: register -> install -> activate -> fetch. **Cache Strategies** determine how requests are handled: Cache First (serve from cache, fallback to network), Network First (try network, fallback to cache), Stale While Revalidate (serve cache immediately, update cache in background). A **Progressive Web App (PWA)** requires a service worker, a web app manifest, and HTTPS.

blocks.output: App works offline. Static assets served instantly from cache. New requests are fetched and added to cache.
Manifest tells the browser how to install the app as a standalone application on mobile home screens.

blocks.question: Which cache strategy serves cached content immediately while fetching an updated version in the background?
blocks.explanation: Stale While Revalidate returns the cached version instantly for speed, then updates the cache with the network response for the next visit.

parts.partTitle: Part 26: Web Security — XSS, CSRF, CSP & Sanitization

blocks.value: Defending Against Injection and Forgery Attacks

**XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)** occurs when untrusted user input is rendered as HTML/JS. Always use `textContent` instead of `innerHTML` for user data, or sanitize with a library like DOMPurify. **CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)** tricks authenticated users into submitting unwanted requests — mitigate with SameSite cookies and anti-CSRF tokens. **CSP (Content Security Policy)** is an HTTP header that whitelists allowed script sources, blocking inline scripts and eval().

blocks.output: textContent prevents script execution. Cookies with HttpOnly are inaccessible to JavaScript. CSP blocks unauthorized script sources.
Custom headers trigger CORS preflight, which cross-origin sites cannot forge without explicit server permission.

blocks.question: Which DOM property safely inserts user-provided text by treating it as plain text rather than HTML?
blocks.explanation: `textContent` sets the text content of a node, automatically escaping HTML special characters so scripts cannot execute.

parts.partTitle: Part 27: Performance Optimization

blocks.value: Core Web Vitals, Lazy Loading, Code Splitting & Critical CSS

Performance is a feature. **Core Web Vitals** measure user experience: **LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)** should be under 2.5s, **FID (First Input Delay)** under 100ms, **CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)** under 0.1. Techniques: use `loading='lazy'` on images below the fold, split JavaScript with dynamic `import()`, inline **Critical CSS** (above-the-fold styles) directly in `<head>`, and defer non-critical scripts. Use `requestIdleCallback` for low-priority work.

blocks.output: Critical path is short. Heavy code loads on demand. Idle time is used for background tasks.

blocks.question: Which Core Web Vital metric measures the time until the largest visible element (like a hero image) is rendered?
blocks.explanation: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures loading performance. It reports the render time of the largest image or text block visible within the viewport.

parts.partTitle: Part 28: TypeScript for Web Developers

blocks.value: Static Typing, Interfaces, Generics, and DOM Type Safety

TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript, catching errors at compile time. Define object shapes with **interfaces** and **type aliases**. Use **generics** for reusable components. TypeScript knows the DOM API — `document.getElementById` returns `HTMLElement | null`, so you must narrow the type (e.g., with `as HTMLInputElement` or type guards) before accessing specific properties.

blocks.output: TypeScript prevents null access, ensures correct property usage, and enables powerful autocomplete in editors.

blocks.question: Which TypeScript syntax asserts that an element is a specific HTML element type?
blocks.explanation: The `as` keyword is a type assertion telling the TypeScript compiler to treat the value as a specific type. It does not perform runtime checking.

parts.partTitle: Part 29: Build Tools, Bundlers & Modern Tooling

blocks.value: Vite, ESBuild, and the Modern Development Workflow

Modern web development relies on build tools to bundle modules, transpile modern syntax, and optimize assets. **Vite** uses native ES modules in development for instant server start and hot module replacement (HMR), then bundles with **Rollup** for production. It handles TypeScript, CSS preprocessing, and asset optimization out of the box. Understand the difference between development servers (fast, unminified) and production builds (minified, tree-shaken, chunked).

blocks.output: Vite configuration with path aliases, SCSS preprocessing, and manual code splitting for optimal caching.
Path aliases keep imports clean. Dynamic imports enable route-level code splitting. Glob imports auto-load collections of files.

blocks.question: Which Vite feature allows a module to be replaced in the browser without a full page reload during development?
blocks.explanation: Hot Module Replacement (HMR) updates only the changed module in the running application, preserving application state and dramatically speeding up the development feedback loop.

parts.partTitle: Part 30: Testing, A11y Audits & DevTools Mastery

blocks.value: Automated Testing, Accessibility, and Browser Debugging

Quality web apps require automated testing. **Unit tests** verify individual functions. **Integration tests** check component interactions. Browser DevTools are essential: the **Elements** panel for DOM/CSS inspection, **Console** for logging and executing JS, **Network** for analyzing requests, **Performance** for profiling, **Lighthouse** for auditing performance, accessibility, SEO, and PWA compliance. Use `axe-core` or Lighthouse CI for automated accessibility checks.

blocks.output: Unit tests verify business logic. E2E tests simulate real user flows across the entire application.
Console timing profiles code. Styled logs improve readability. $0 references the selected element.

blocks.question: Which built-in browser tool provides automated audits for Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, SEO, and PWA?
blocks.explanation: Lighthouse is an open-source, automated tool for improving the quality of web pages. It runs audits and generates a report with scores and actionable recommendations.
